title: Water on the desert road (Acts 8:26–40)
hook: a powerful man with a scroll he can't make sense of, and a stranger running beside his chariot
tomorrow: what fell from Saul's eyes, and whose hands did it take?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simon reached for his money, and Peter called the Spirit the gift of God. The line: not for sale.

A lease, a medical form, the poem from English class everyone else seems to get: some reading is hard to do alone. Acts puts a powerful man in exactly that spot. On the desert road down from Jerusalem to Gaza rolls a chariot. In it sits a man of Ethiopia, in charge of all the treasure of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. He has been to Jerusalem to worship, and he's reading the prophet Isaiah aloud as he rides. The Spirit tells Philip: "Go near, and join thyself to this chariot."
screen: `SOME READING IS HARD ALONE.` → `A QUEEN'S TREASURER, READING ISAIAH.` → `GO NEAR.`

segments.voice: Philip runs up and asks, "Understandest thou what thou readest?" The answer is disarmingly honest: "How can I, except some man should guide me?" He invites Philip up. Philip "began at the same scripture," tells him about Jesus, and when they pass water by the road, the man is baptized. Then Philip is gone, and "he went on his way rejoicing." Christians still argue about that question in the chariot. One view: scripture is clear enough that an ordinary reader can understand what matters most. The Westminster Confession, a Reformed statement of faith, says in its first chapter that not only the learned but the unlearned can reach a sufficient understanding. Its best case: the Bible was written for ordinary people, and nobody should need permission to open it. The other view: scripture is read best inside the church that carried it. Catholic teaching says the task of authentically interpreting it belongs to the Church's living teaching office. Its best case: even a royal treasurer couldn't make sense of Isaiah alone, and a guide keeps a reader from building a private Bible. Notice what's in the chariot. The man owns the scroll and is reading it himself. He also asks for help. Acts doesn't settle the argument. It sits both on one seat, and sends the reader home glad.
screen: `HOW CAN I, EXCEPT SOME MAN GUIDE ME?` · `ONE VIEW: CLEAR ENOUGH TO READ ALONE.` · `THE OTHER: READ IT WITH THE CHURCH.` · `ONE SCROLL, ONE SEAT, TWO READERS.` · then, large: `ON HIS WAY REJOICING.`

segments.voice: Choose one short line of scripture, or any line you carry but don't fully understand. Send it to someone you trust with one question: what do you hear in this? Then set the phone face down for the sit, and let the line rest in you while the answer is on its way.
Water on the desert road. Where the man from Ethiopia asked, what doth hinder me to be baptized?

howItsDone: Christians read scripture alone and together: in personal devotions, in small groups around a kitchen table, and in church, where it is read aloud and explained.

fork.setup: your cousin reads the Bible on her own and says she doesn't need any church explaining it. what's the strongest case for the other view?
options: even a royal treasurer asked for a guide, and one keeps you from a private Bible.
the Bible is too hard for ordinary people to read at all.
only clergy are really allowed to read it properly.
fork.reveal: the best case for reading with a guide isn't that readers are dull. the man in the chariot read Isaiah himself, and still asked: how can I, except some man should guide me?

chat.meaning: The man owned the scroll and read it himself, and still asked, How can I, except some man should guide me? Acts holds both.

v3 debate: two views inside the tradition, each given its best case. Westminster Confession 1.7 paraphrased ('not only the learned, but the unlearned ... may attain unto a sufficient understanding'); Dei Verbum 10 paraphrased ('the task of authentically interpreting the word of God ... has been entrusted exclusively to the living teaching office of the Church'). Confirm both paraphrases and that Reformed and Catholic readers find their view fairly stated. Orthodox reading with the church fathers was left out for length; a Keeper may want it added.
'reading Isaiah aloud' rests on Acts 8:30 (Philip 'heard him read').
v3 myth item (the popular misreading): the man couldn't read. He was reading; he asked for help understanding.
